claim: Vesicular neurotransmitter transporters (VNTs) mediate the selective uptake and enrichment of small-molecule neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles (SVs).
source: Vesicular neurotransmitter transporters (VNTs) mediate the selective uptake and enrichment of small-molecule neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles (SVs) and are therefore a major determinant of the synaptic output of specific neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about VNTs and their function.

claim: VNTs are a major determinant of the synaptic output of specific neurons.
source: Vesicular neurotransmitter transporters (VNTs) mediate the selective uptake and enrichment of small-molecule neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles (SVs) and are therefore a major determinant of the synaptic output of specific neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established role of VNTs in neurotransmitter uptake.

claim: Localization profiling of 361 solute carrier (SLC) transporters in neurons revealed 40 possible vesicular transporter candidates.
source: To identify novel VNTs expressed on SVs (thus identifying new neurotransmitters and/or neuromodulators), we conducted localization profiling of 361 solute carrier (SLC) transporters tagging with a fluorescent protein in neurons, which revealed 40 possible candidates through comparison with a known SV marker.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the localization screening described in the manuscript.

claim: Proteomics analysis of immunoisolated SVs identified seven transporters that overlapped with the localization screen candidates.
source: We parallelly performed proteomics analysis of immunoisolated SVs and identified seven transporters in overlap.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental proteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SLC35D3 localizes to synaptic vesicles.
source: Ultrastructural analysis further supported that one of the transporters, SLC35D3, localized to SVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ultrastructural analysis using APEX2-based EM as shown in the manuscript.

claim: UDP-glucose is the principal substrate for SLC35D3.
source: Finally, by combining metabolite profiling with a radiolabeled substrate transport assay, we identified UDP-glucose as the principal substrate for SLC35D3.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite profiling and radiolabeled transport assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All VNTs identified to date belong to the Solute Carrier (SLC) superfamily of membrane transport proteins.
source: All VNTs identified to date belong to the Solute Carrier (SLC) superfamily of membrane transport proteins, the second-largest group of membrane proteins in the human proteome, with more than 400 members spanning 65 subfamilies (http://slc.bioparadigms.org/) (Hediger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hediger et al., 2013.

claim: The SLC superfamily is the second-largest group of membrane proteins in the human proteome.
source: All VNTs identified to date belong to the Solute Carrier (SLC) superfamily of membrane transport proteins, the second-largest group of membrane proteins in the human proteome, with more than 400 members spanning 65 subfamilies (http://slc.bioparadigms.org/) (Hediger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hediger et al., 2013.

claim: The SLC superfamily has more than 400 members spanning 65 subfamilies.
source: All VNTs identified to date belong to the Solute Carrier (SLC) superfamily of membrane transport proteins, the second-largest group of membrane proteins in the human proteome, with more than 400 members spanning 65 subfamilies (http://slc.bioparadigms.org/) (Hediger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hediger et al., 2013.

claim: Approximately 30% of the 400 SLC transporters are either uncharacterized or orphan transporters.
source: Strikingly, approximately 30% of these 400 transporters are either uncharacterized or orphan transporters (César-Razquin et al., 2015; Perland and Fredriksson, 2017), providing the opportunity to identify novel VNTs and their cognate substrates, thus identifying new neurotransmitters and/or neuromodulators.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to César-Razquin et al., 2015 and Perland and Fredriksson, 2017.

claim: VGLUT and VGAT transport glutamate and GABA, respectively.
source: In the nervous system, vesicular neurotransmitter transporters (VNTs) such as VGLUT and VGAT (which transport glutamate and GABA, respectively) are essential for the transport of small-molecule neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles (SVs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about these specific transporters.

claim: VNTs determine the category, amount, and transport kinetics of neurotransmitters.
source: These selective transporters determine the category, amount, and transport kinetics of neurotransmitters, thereby establishing the molecular basis of the underlying chemical neurotransmission (Blakely and Edwards, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blakely and Edwards, 2012.

claim: Known vesicular transporters such as VGLUT and VAChT had relatively high co-localization ratio with SYP-EGFP (50–80% co-localization).
source: As expected, known synaptic vesicular transporters such as VGLUT and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) had relatively high co-localization ratio with SYP-EGFP (50–80% co-localization) (Figure 1C,E), whereas markers of non-vesicular organelles such as the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria had relatively low co-localization ratio (10–20%) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1E.

claim: Markers of non-vesicular organelles such as the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria had relatively low co-localization ratio (10–20%) with SYP-EGFP.
source: As expected, known synaptic vesicular transporters such as VGLUT and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) had relatively high co-localization ratio with SYP-EGFP (50–80% co-localization) (Figure 1C,E), whereas markers of non-vesicular organelles such as the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria had relatively low co-localization ratio (10–20%) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2 had a co-localization ratio of approximately 70% with SYP-EGFP.
source: Among these candidates, a subset of SLC35 transporters, including SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2, had a co-localization ratio of approximately 70% with SYP-EGFP (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: SLC35A1, SLC35E1, and SLC35E2 localized primarily to organelles in the soma and had relatively low co-localization ratio (10–20%) with SYP-EGFP.
source: In contrast, other members of the same subfamily, such as SLC35A1, SLC35E1, and SLC35E2, localized primarily to organelles in the soma and had relatively low co-localization ratio (10–20%) (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1G.

claim: The proteins enriched in the anti-SYP sample covered more than 60% of the 110 proteins in the SV proteome listed in the SynGO database.
source: The proteins enriched in the anti-SYP sample covered more than 60% of the 110 proteins in the SV proteome listed in the SynGO database (Koopmans et al., 2019), including known VNTs, vesicular ATPase subunits, and a number of other SV markers (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2D-F and comparison with the SynGO database.

claim: Only 8.0% and 2.2% of the proteins in the mitochondrial and Golgi apparatus proteome, respectively, were present in the anti-SYP sample.
source: Conversely, only 8.0% and 2.2% of the proteins in the mitochondrial and Golgi apparatus proteome, respectively, were present in the anti-SYP sample (Figure 2F), indicating minimal contamination by these organelles; as an additional control, we found very little overlap between the proteins in the anti-SYP sample and the entire mouse proteome in the UniProt database (UniProt Consortium et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Twenty SLC transporters were identified among the SV-associated proteins, including SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2.
source: We then focused on SLC transporters and identified 20 SLC transporters, including SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2, among the SV-associated proteins (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The abundance of SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2 was similar to known VNTs, including VAChT and VMAT2.
source: The abundance of these three transporters was similar to known VNTs, including VAChT and the monoamine transporter VMAT2 (Figure 2G), even though VAChT was below the threshold for significance (p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Seven transporters were present in both the localization screen and the SV proteome datasets, including SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2.
source: Comparing the putative vesicular transporters identified in our localization screen with the SLC transporters identified in the SV proteome revealed a total of seven transporters present in both datasets, including the three SLC35 family members (i.e., SLC35D3, SLC35F1, and SLC35G2) identified above (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of localization and proteomics data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The other four transporters present in both datasets were SLC5A7, SLC6A7, SLC6A17, and SLC30A3.
source: The other four transporters were previously reported to localize to SVs including the choline transporter SLC5A7 (Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003), the proline transporter SLC6A7 (Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999), the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A17 (Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999), and the zinc transporter SLC30A3 (Wenzel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SLC5A7 is a choline transporter previously reported to localize to SVs.
source: The other four transporters were previously reported to localize to SVs including the choline transporter SLC5A7 (Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003), the proline transporter SLC6A7 (Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999), the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A17 (Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999), and the zinc transporter SLC30A3 (Wenzel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003.

claim: SLC6A7 is a proline transporter previously reported to localize to SVs.
source: The other four transporters were previously reported to localize to SVs including the choline transporter SLC5A7 (Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003), the proline transporter SLC6A7 (Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999), the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A17 (Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999), and the zinc transporter SLC30A3 (Wenzel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999.

claim: SLC6A17 is a neutral amino acid transporter previously reported to localize to SVs.
source: The other four transporters were previously reported to localize to SVs including the choline transporter SLC5A7 (Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003), the proline transporter SLC6A7 (Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999), the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A17 (Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999), and the zinc transporter SLC30A3 (Wenzel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999.

claim: SLC30A3 is a zinc transporter previously reported to localize to SVs.
source: The other four transporters were previously reported to localize to SVs including the choline transporter SLC5A7 (Ferguson et al., 2003; Nakata et al., 2004; Ribeiro et al., 2003), the proline transporter SLC6A7 (Crump et al., 1999; Renick et al., 1999), the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A17 (Fischer et al., 1999; Masson et al., 1999), and the zinc transporter SLC30A3 (Wenzel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wenzel et al., 1997.

claim: Neurons transfected with either VGLUT1-APEX2 or SLC35D3-APEX2 had two distinct populations of SVs based on electron density.
source: Importantly, neurons transfected with either VGLUT1-APEX2 (Figure 3D) or SLC35D3-APEX2 (Figure 3E) had two distinct populations of SVs based on electron density, demonstrating that SLC35D3 could localize to SVs in cultured neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: SLC35D3 could localize to SVs in cultured neurons.
source: Importantly, neurons transfected with either VGLUT1-APEX2 (Figure 3D) or SLC35D3-APEX2 (Figure 3E) had two distinct populations of SVs based on electron density, demonstrating that SLC35D3 could localize to SVs in cultured neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Overexpressing SLC35A2 resulted in a >100% increase in UDP-galactose in organelles.
source: Profiling the relative abundance of specific nucleotide sugars in organelles prepared from control cells and SLC35A2-overexpressing (SLC35A2OE) cells revealed a >100% increase in the substrate UDP-galactose in SLC35A2OE organelles (Figure 4F,G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 4F, 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Overexpressing SLC35A2 resulted in 60% higher levels of UDP-glucose in organelles.
source: Interestingly, we also detected 60% higher levels of UDP-glucose in SLC35A2OE cells, indicating a previously unknown substrate of the SLC35A2 transporter; in contrast, we found that the SLC35A2 substrate UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine did not appear to be enriched in SLC35A2OE cells, possibly due to limitations in separating UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine and UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine in our HPLC–MS setup (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: UDP-glucose is a previously unknown substrate of the SLC35A2 transporter.
source: Interestingly, we also detected 60% higher levels of UDP-glucose in SLC35A2OE cells, indicating a previously unknown substrate of the SLC35A2 transporter; in contrast, we found that the SLC35A2 substrate UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine did not appear to be enriched in SLC35A2OE cells, possibly due to limitations in separating UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine and UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine in our HPLC–MS setup (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the metabolite profiling data showing increased UDP-glucose in SLC35A2OE cells.

claim: Overexpressing SLC35D3 resulted in a 40% increase in UDP-glucose in organelles.
source: Our analysis revealed a 40% increase in UDP-glucose and a 30% increase in CMP-sialic acid in SLC35D3OE organelles compared to control organelles (Figure 4H,I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that these two nucleotide sugars might be substrates of the SLC35D3 transporter.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 4H, 4I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Overexpressing SLC35D3 resulted in a 30% increase in CMP-sialic acid in organelles.
source: Our analysis revealed a 40% increase in UDP-glucose and a 30% increase in CMP-sialic acid in SLC35D3OE organelles compared to control organelles (Figure 4H,I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that these two nucleotide sugars might be substrates of the SLC35D3 transporter.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 4H, 4I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells expressing human SLC35D3 had a nearly onefold increase in UDP-glucose transport.
source: Importantly, cells expressing human SLC35D3 had a nearly onefold increase in UDP-glucose transport, but no significant change in the transport of UDP-galactose or UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine; similar results were obtained from the cells expressed the mouse SLC35D3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by radiolabeled transport assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells expressing human SLC35D3 had no significant change in the transport of UDP-galactose or UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine.
source: Importantly, cells expressing human SLC35D3 had a nearly onefold increase in UDP-glucose transport, but no significant change in the transport of UDP-galactose or UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine; similar results were obtained from the cells expressed the mouse SLC35D3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by radiolabeled transport assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells expressing mouse SLC35D3 showed similar transport results to cells expressing human SLC35D3.
source: Importantly, cells expressing human SLC35D3 had a nearly onefold increase in UDP-glucose transport, but no significant change in the transport of UDP-galactose or UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine; similar results were obtained from the cells expressed the mouse SLC35D3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by radiolabeled transport assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Non-radiolabeled UDP-glucose virtually eliminated the transport of radiolabeled UDP-glucose by SLC35D3.
source: We found that non-radiolabeled UDP-glucose – but not the structurally similar UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine – virtually eliminated the transport of radiolabeled UDP-glucose (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine did not eliminate the transport of radiolabeled UDP-glucose by SLC35D3.
source: We found that non-radiolabeled UDP-glucose – but not the structurally similar UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine – virtually eliminated the transport of radiolabeled UDP-glucose (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CMP-sialic acid did not reduce the transport of UDP-glucose by SLC35D3.
source: Interestingly, CMP-sialic acid did not reduce the transport of UDP-glucose (Figure 5C), even though this nucleotide sugar was increased – albeit to a lesser extent than UDP-glucose – in the organelles of cells expressing SLC35D3 (see Figure 4I), indicating that CMP-sialic acid may not be a direct substrate of SLC35D3 but may have been indirectly increased on its abundance as shown by metabolite profiling.
evidence: This claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CMP-sialic acid may not be a direct substrate of SLC35D3.
source: Interestingly, CMP-sialic acid did not reduce the transport of UDP-glucose (Figure 5C), even though this nucleotide sugar was increased – albeit to a lesser extent than UDP-glucose – in the organelles of cells expressing SLC35D3 (see Figure 4I), indicating that CMP-sialic acid may not be a direct substrate of SLC35D3 but may have been indirectly increased on its abundance as shown by metabolite profiling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the competition assay and metabolite profiling data.

claim: UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3 has a time constant of 2.9 min.
source: We also measured the time course and dose dependence of UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3, revealing a time constant of 2.9 min (Figure 5D) and a Km value of 0.87 μM (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by time course data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3 has a Km value of 0.87 μM.
source: We also measured the time course and dose dependence of UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3, revealing a time constant of 2.9 min (Figure 5D) and a Km value of 0.87 μM (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells.
source: We found that N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone), and nigericin significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that the electrochemical proton gradient contributes – at least in part – to the driving force.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FCCP significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells.
source: We found that N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone), and nigericin significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that the electrochemical proton gradient contributes – at least in part – to the driving force.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Nigericin significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells.
source: We found that N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone), and nigericin significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that the electrochemical proton gradient contributes – at least in part – to the driving force.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The electrochemical proton gradient contributes to the driving force for UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3.
source: We found that N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone), and nigericin significantly reduced UDP-glucose transport in SLC35D3-expressing cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that the electrochemical proton gradient contributes – at least in part – to the driving force.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pharmacological inhibition data.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 did not reduce UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3.
source: Interestingly, Bafilomycin A1 did not reduce the transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data.

claim: UDP-glucose plays an essential role in glycosylation in both the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus.
source: The nucleotide sugar uridine diphosphate glucose (UDP-glucose) plays an essential role in glycosylation in both the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus (Moremen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moremen et al., 2012.

claim: The release of UDP-glucose into the extracellular space was detected previously using an enzyme-based method.
source: Interestingly, the release of UDP-glucose into the extracellular space was detected previously using an enzyme-based method (Lazarowski et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lazarowski et al., 2003.

claim: The release of UDP-glucose from 1231N1 cells requires both Ca2+ signaling and the secretory pathway.
source: Subsequent experiments with 1231N1 cells (an astrocytoma cell line) showed that the release of UDP-glucose requires both Ca2+ signaling and the secretory pathway, as the release was inhibited by the Ca2+ chelator BAPTA and the Golgi apparatus blocker brefeldin A (Kreda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kreda et al., 2008.

claim: The SLC35 family contains 31 members, including 20 orphan transporters.
source: Nucleotide sugars are transported into subcellular organelles by the SLC35 family, which contains 31 members, including 20 orphan transporters (Caffaro and Hirschberg, 2006; Ishida and Kawakita, 2004; Song, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caffaro and Hirschberg, 2006; Ishida and Kawakita, 2004; Song, 2013.

claim: Knocking out an SLC35 homolog in yeast decreased the release of UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine.
source: Importantly, the level of nucleotide sugars released by cells can be manipulated by changing the expression of SLC35 transporters; for example, knocking out an SLC35 homolog in yeast decreased the release of UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine, whereas overexpressing human SLC35D2 in airway epithelial cells increased UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine release (Sesma et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sesma et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpressing human SLC35D2 in airway epithelial cells increased UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine release.
source: Importantly, the level of nucleotide sugars released by cells can be manipulated by changing the expression of SLC35 transporters; for example, knocking out an SLC35 homolog in yeast decreased the release of UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine, whereas overexpressing human SLC35D2 in airway epithelial cells increased UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine release (Sesma et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sesma et al., 2009.

claim: SLC35D3 is expressed primarily in striatal neurons that project to the substantia nigra and the globus pallidus externa in the brain.
source: SLC35D3 is expressed primarily in striatal neurons that project to the substantia nigra and the globus pallidus externa in the brain (Lobo et al., 2006), and mice with a recessive mutation in the SLC35D3 gene have decreased motor activity, impaired energy expenditure, and develop obesity (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lobo et al., 2006.

claim: Mice with a recessive mutation in the SLC35D3 gene have decreased motor activity, impaired energy expenditure, and develop obesity.
source: SLC35D3 is expressed primarily in striatal neurons that project to the substantia nigra and the globus pallidus externa in the brain (Lobo et al., 2006), and mice with a recessive mutation in the SLC35D3 gene have decreased motor activity, impaired energy expenditure, and develop obesity (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: UDP-sugars, including UDP-glucose, could serve as the ligand of the purinergic receptor P2Y14.
source: Interestingly, previous studies regarding G protein‒coupled receptors (GPCRs) found that UDP-sugars, including UDP-glucose, could serve as the ligand of the purinergic receptor P2Y14 (Chambers et al., 2000; Freeman et al., 2001), indicating that nucleotide sugars may function as extracellular signaling molecules, a notion supported by the fact that the P2Y14 receptor is widely expressed in a variety of brain regions and cell types (Chambers et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2000; Freeman et al., 2001.

claim: The P2Y14 receptor is widely expressed in a variety of brain regions and cell types.
source: Interestingly, previous studies regarding G protein‒coupled receptors (GPCRs) found that UDP-sugars, including UDP-glucose, could serve as the ligand of the purinergic receptor P2Y14 (Chambers et al., 2000; Freeman et al., 2001), indicating that nucleotide sugars may function as extracellular signaling molecules, a notion supported by the fact that the P2Y14 receptor is widely expressed in a variety of brain regions and cell types (Chambers et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Zeisel et al., 2018.

claim: The P2Y14 receptor is coupled primarily with the Gαi protein.
source: The P2Y14 receptor is coupled primarily with the Gαi protein (Chambers et al., 2000; Inoue et al., 2019), which does not elicit an excitatory downstream calcium signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2000; Inoue et al., 2019.

claim: SLC35D3 can be localized to secretory organelles in platelets.
source: SLC35D3 can be localized to secretory organelles in platelets, and mutations on SLC35D3 lead to malfunction of the secretory organelles in platelets of mice, which resembles HPS syndrome that causes bleeding in humans (Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations on SLC35D3 lead to malfunction of the secretory organelles in platelets of mice.
source: SLC35D3 can be localized to secretory organelles in platelets, and mutations on SLC35D3 lead to malfunction of the secretory organelles in platelets of mice, which resembles HPS syndrome that causes bleeding in humans (Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012.

claim: UDP-sugars can mediate vasoconstriction of the porcine coronary artery through the P2Y14 receptor.
source: Moreover, UDP-sugars can mediate vasoconstriction of the porcine coronary artery through the P2Y14 receptor (Abbas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abbas et al., 2018.

claim: Electron microscopy offers vastly superior resolution (on the order of 1 nm in biological samples) compared to optical imaging (on the order of 200–300 nm).
source: Electron microscopy (EM) is the gold standard to obtain ultrastructural information since it offers the vastly superior resolution (on the order of 1 nm in biological samples) compared to the resolution of optical imaging (on the order of 200–300 nm) (Fernández-Suárez and Ting, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fernández-Suárez and Ting, 2008.

claim: APEX2 is a highly efficient proximity-based EM tag suitable for determining the subcellular localization of proteins of interest.
source: APEX2, an enhanced variant of ascorbate peroxidase, is a highly efficient proximity-based EM tag (Lam et al., 2015) suitable for determining the subcellular localization of proteins of interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lam et al., 2015.

claim: Of the 223 SLC transporters that trafficked to neurites, 134 showed overlap with SYP-EGFP.
source: Of the 223 SLC transporters that trafficked to neurites, 134 showed overlap with SYP-EGFP and were analyzed further by quantifying the co-localization ratio between the red and green fluorescent signals (Figure 1A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization screening data shown in Figure 1A and 1E.

claim: The co-localization ratio between SLC35D3 and SYP in lentivirus infected neurons was approximately 60%.
source: The co-localization ratio between SLC35D3 and SYP (SV marker) was ~60%, which is similar to that in the plasmid transfected neurons (~70%).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data from lentivirus infected neurons.

claim: The co-localization ratio between SLC35D3 and Chg A (secretory granule marker) was approximately 30%.
source: Given SYP may also be localized to secretory granules, we co-immunostained a secretory granule marker Chg A and found that the co-localization ratio between SLC35D3 and Chg A was ~30%.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data.

claim: SLC35D3 with relatively low expression level has a higher possibility to localize to synaptic vesicles than to secretory granules.
source: Taken together, SLC35D3 with relatively low expression level has a higher possibility to localize to synaptic vesicles than to secretory granules.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data comparing SYP and Chg A.

claim: SLC35D3 is enriched from P2' (crude synaptosome) to LP2 (crude SVs) fraction during differential centrifugation.
source: With the progress of differential centrifugation, we observed enrichment of SLC35D3 from P2' (crude synaptosome) to LP2 (crude SVs) fraction, which is similar to known SV markers VGLUT1 and SYP.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential centrifugation data.

claim: SLC35D3 is less likely to be a classic ER/Golgi transporter.
source: In summary, these data corroborate the view that SLC35D3 is less likely to be a classic ER/Golgi transporter and tends to localize to SVs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential centrifugation data.

claim: SLC35A2 is known to transport UDP-galactose and UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine.
source: To test the sensitivity of this deorphanization strategy, we generated a stable cell line overexpressing EGFP-tagged SLC35A2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which is known to transport the nucleotide sugars including UDP-galactose and UDP-N-acetyl-galactosamine (Ishida et al., 1996; Segawa et al., 2002; Sun-Wada et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ishida et al., 1996; Segawa et al., 2002; Sun-Wada et al., 1998.

claim: Several UDP-sugars partially inhibited UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3 but were not enriched in the metabolite profiling.
source: In addition, several other UDP-sugars partially inhibited transport activity but were not enriched in the metabolite profiling, possibly by competing with UDP-glucose on the transporter's substrate-binding pocket.
evidence: This claim is supported by competition assay data and metabolite profiling data.

claim: SLC35A3 is an ER/Golgi localized UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine transporter.
source: To compare the transport mechanism of SLC35D3 with a canonical ER/Golgi localized SLC35 transporter, we investigated the pharmacological properties of SLC35A3, which is an ER/Golgi localized UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine transporter (Ishida et al., 1999; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ishida et al., 1999.

claim: Pharmacological treatment including proton uncouplers did not significantly inhibit UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine transport by SLC35A3.
source: We found the pharmacological treatment including proton uncouplers did not significantly inhibit UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine transport, indicating SLC35A3 may have a different transport mechanism compared with SLC35D3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SLC35A3 may have a different transport mechanism compared with SLC35D3.
source: We found the pharmacological treatment including proton uncouplers did not significantly inhibit UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine transport, indicating SLC35A3 may have a different transport mechanism compared with SLC35D3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pharmacological inhibition data.

claim: VMAT2 could localize to both synaptic vesicles and large dense-core vesicles in neurons.
source: Taking the well-known vesicular transporter VMAT2 as an example, it could localize to both synaptic vesicles and large dense-core vesicles in neurons (Nirenberg et al., 1996), as well as secretory granules in endocrine cells of the peripheral system (Weihe et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nirenberg et al., 1996.

claim: VMAT2 could localize to secretory granules in endocrine cells of the peripheral system.
source: Taking the well-known vesicular transporter VMAT2 as an example, it could localize to both synaptic vesicles and large dense-core vesicles in neurons (Nirenberg et al., 1996), as well as secretory granules in endocrine cells of the peripheral system (Weihe et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weihe et al., 1994.

claim: SLC17A9 has been reported to play a role in vesicular ATP release.
source: For example, the vesicular nucleotide transporter SLC17A9 has been reported to play a role in vesicular ATP release (Sawada et al., 2008), but was not identified in our proteomics analyses of SVs, consistent with reports by other groups (Grønborg et al., 2010; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sawada et al., 2008.

claim: SLC17A9 was not identified in the proteomics analyses of SVs in this study.
source: For example, the vesicular nucleotide transporter SLC17A9 has been reported to play a role in vesicular ATP release (Sawada et al., 2008), but was not identified in our proteomics analyses of SVs, consistent with reports by other groups (Grønborg et al., 2010; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomics data from this study.

claim: SLC10A4 is a vesicular transporter.
source: Similarly, our analysis did not identify SLC10A4, another vesicular transporter (Larhammar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larhammar et al., 2015.

claim: SLC10A4 was not identified in the proteomics analyses of SVs in this study.
source: Similarly, our analysis did not identify SLC10A4, another vesicular transporter (Larhammar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomics data from this study.

claim: SLC35G2 was recently reported in SV proteomics using an improved workflow.
source: SLC35G2 was recently reported in SV proteomics using an improved workflow (Taoufiq et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taoufiq et al., 2020.

claim: SLC35D3 has an even lower protein abundance compared with SLC35G2.
source: Interestingly, SLC35D3 was not simultaneously identified, potentially due to a few reasons: (1) the proteome may vary across different species at different ages (SD rats at 4–6 weeks vs C57BL6 mice at 6–8 weeks); (2) SLC35D3 has an even lower protein abundance compared with SLC35G2 (Figure 2G), which is more challenging for detection; and (3) different purification strategies may lead to differences in SV pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: SLC35F5 was found to be enriched in VGAT-positive SVs instead of VGLUT1-positive SVs.
source: For example, another SLC35 family member, SLC35F5, was found to be enriched in VGAT-positive SVs instead of VGLUT1-positive SVs, even though the majority of the two proteomes were highly similar (Boyken et al., 2013; Grønborg et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyken et al., 2013; Grønborg et al., 2010.

claim: UDP-glucose is generally synthesized and exists in the cytoplasm.
source: The substrate of SLC35D3, UDP-glucose, is generally synthesized and exists in the cytoplasm (Hirschberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hirschberg et al., 1998.

claim: UDP-glucose can be degraded by ecto-nucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterases (E-NPPs).
source: After the extracellular signaling process, UDP-glucose can be degraded by ecto-nucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterases (E-NPPs), which is widely known to metabolize nucleoside triphosphates (Lazarowski and Harden, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lazarowski and Harden, 2015.

claim: E-NPPs are widely known to metabolize nucleoside triphosphates.
source: After the extracellular signaling process, UDP-glucose can be degraded by ecto-nucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterases (E-NPPs), which is widely known to metabolize nucleoside triphosphates (Lazarowski and Harden, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lazarowski and Harden, 2015.

claim: UDP-glucose will be transported into SVs in SLC35D3-positive neurons and undergo regulated exocytosis upon stimulations.
source: In our hypothesis, UDP-glucose will be transported into SVs in SLC35D3-positive neurons and undergo regulated exocytosis upon stimulations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Nucleotide sugars may function as extracellular signaling molecules.
source: Interestingly, previous studies regarding G protein‒coupled receptors (GPCRs) found that UDP-sugars, including UDP-glucose, could serve as the ligand of the purinergic receptor P2Y14 (Chambers et al., 2000; Freeman et al., 2001), indicating that nucleotide sugars may function as extracellular signaling molecules, a notion supported by the fact that the P2Y14 receptor is widely expressed in a variety of brain regions and cell types (Chambers et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fact that UDP-sugars can bind to P2Y14 receptor.

claim: The Gαi protein does not elicit an excitatory downstream calcium signal.
source: The P2Y14 receptor is coupled primarily with the Gαi protein (Chambers et al., 2000; Inoue et al., 2019), which does not elicit an excitatory downstream calcium signal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gαi protein signaling.

claim: Mutations on SLC35D3 resemble HPS syndrome that causes bleeding in humans.
source: SLC35D3 can be localized to secretory organelles in platelets, and mutations on SLC35D3 lead to malfunction of the secretory organelles in platelets of mice, which resembles HPS syndrome that causes bleeding in humans (Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chintala et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2012.

claim: There can be preserved proton electrochemical gradient in SVs after the acute application of Bafilomycin A1.
source: There can be preserved proton electrochemical gradient in SVs after the acute application of Bafilomycin A1, as indicated by a previous work using pH-dependent quantum dots to study SV Kiss and Run (K and R) and full-collapse fusion (FCF) (Zhang et al., 2009), which may support UDP-glucose transport by SLC35D3.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The transport activity of GDP-mannose by a yeast homolog of the nucleotide–sugar transporters was neither sensitive to CCCP nor valinomycin.
source: Moreover, the transport activity of GDP-mannose by a yeast homolog of the nucleotide–sugar transporters was neither sensitive to CCCP nor valinomycin (Parker and Newstead, 2017), which also suggested different transport mechanisms among nucleotide–sugar transporters.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parker and Newstead, 2017.

claim: Different transport mechanisms exist among nucleotide–sugar transporters.
source: Moreover, the transport activity of GDP-mannose by a yeast homolog of the nucleotide–sugar transporters was neither sensitive to CCCP nor valinomycin (Parker and Newstead, 2017), which also suggested different transport mechanisms among nucleotide–sugar transporters.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of pharmacological properties of different nucleotide-sugar transporters.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 inhibits V-ATPase that indirectly affects the maintenance of proton electrochemical gradient.
source: Unlike the proton uncouplers that directly abolish the proton electrochemical gradient, Bafilomycin A1 inhibits V-ATPase that indirectly affects the maintenance of proton electrochemical gradient (Yoshimori et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yoshimori et al., 1991.

claim: Proton uncouplers directly abolish the proton electrochemical gradient.
source: Unlike the proton uncouplers that directly abolish the proton electrochemical gradient, Bafilomycin A1 inhibits V-ATPase that indirectly affects the maintenance of proton electrochemical gradient (Yoshimori et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about proton uncouplers.

claim: The electrochemical proton gradient has been reported to drive the activity of known VNTs.
source: Lastly, we examined the role of the electrochemical proton gradient on SLC35D3 activity, as this gradient has been reported to drive the activity of known VNTs (Edwards, 2007; Van Liefferinge et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards, 2007; Van Liefferinge et al., 2013.

claim: The lowest expression level of epitope-tagged SLC35D3 was achieved using lentivirus, which was approximately 40% compared with plasmid transfection.
source: The lowest expression level of epitope-tagged SLC35D3 was achieved using lentivirus, which was ~40% compared with plasmid transfection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression level data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 1B.
